sections.overview: Bidessus unistriatus is a minute aquatic beetle in the diving-beetle family Dytiscidae. It belongs to Bidessus, a genus of very small dytiscids; unlike the familiar large great diving beetle Dytiscus marginalis, this species is only a few millimetres long.
sections.identification: It is about 2 mm long and dark brown. Reliable identification from other tiny diving beetles requires magnification and examination of diagnostic structures; the single-grooved appearance behind its English common name is not by itself a complete field key.
sections.habitat: In Britain it is recorded from lowland stagnant pools, marl pits and slow drainage channels, often at sparsely vegetated margins. It has not been reported from brackish water in the cited regional account, despite some coastal occurrences.
sections.diet: As a predatory diving beetle, it belongs to a family whose adults and larvae generally hunt small aquatic animals. Species-specific prey observations were not detailed in the regional account consulted, so a narrower diet is not assigned here.
sections.behavior: The species is aquatic and associated with still or very slow water. British observations indicate that it can fly, which may help it move among suitable pools, although flight frequency is not quantified in the sources used.
sections.reproduction: The sources consulted did not provide species-specific courtship, egg-laying or development details. As a beetle it undergoes complete metamorphosis, but the timing and precise stages in this species are left unspecified here.
sections.ecology: It depends on small, lowland freshwater habitats and is recorded in England from scattered, increasingly isolated localities. Drainage, water-quality changes and coastal saline intrusion are identified as pressures on the British populations.
sections.conservation: The British review describes a severe contraction from a formerly wider English distribution and highlights risk from saline intrusion near Hickling Broad. This regional evidence does not establish a global IUCN category; national status should not be mistaken for the species’ worldwide status.
